subject: Medicine
summary: Leishmaniasis is a parasitic disease transmitted by sandflies, presenting as cutaneous, mucocutaneous, or visceral forms. Diagnosis relies on clinical clues and parasite detection; treatment targets the parasite while managing complications.

sections.p: Leishmaniasis is caused by Leishmania spp., transmitted by sandfly bites. Visceral disease (kala-azar) shows fever, weight loss, splenomegaly; cutaneous lesions are ulcerative. Diagnosis requires parasite identification (skin smear, splenic aspirate) or serology (rK39).

t.b: Detects antibodies; positive suggests visceral leishmaniasis, but false‑negative in early disease.
Confirms amastigotes; high sensitivity but invasive.
Detects parasite DNA; useful when microscopy is negative.

sections.p: Visceral leishmaniasis is staged by clinical severity: mild (fever, mild splenomegaly), moderate (anemia, thrombocytopenia), severe (splenic rupture, septicemia). Cutaneous disease is staged by ulcer size and number.
Primary cause is sandfly bite in endemic areas. Co‑factors include HIV, malnutrition, and chronic infections such as tuberculosis or malaria, which worsen outcomes.

Visceral leishmaniasis presents with prolonged fever, weight loss, pallor, splenomegaly, and pancytopenia. Cutaneous forms start as papules that ulcerate; mucocutaneous disease involves nasal or oral mucosa.
Key tests confirm parasite presence and assess severity. When resources are limited, a simple smear and CBC can guide management.

t.b: Answers if anemia or thrombocytopenia is present; low platelets suggest bleeding risk.
Screening tool; positive supports diagnosis when microscopy unavailable.

sections.p: Urgent complications include splenic rupture, severe anemia, septicemia, and post‑kala‑azar dermal leishmaniasis. Red flags: sudden abdominal pain, bleeding, altered consciousness.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden abdominal pain (splenic rupture), severe bleeding, confusion, or any sign of septic shock

faq.q: Can leishmaniasis be transmitted by blood transfusion?
faq.a: Yes, especially visceral leishmaniasis; screening of donors in endemic areas is advised.

faq.q: Is there a vaccine for leishmaniasis?
faq.a: No licensed vaccine exists; prevention relies on vector control and early treatment.
Yes, relapse and post‑kala‑azar dermal leishmaniasis can occur, especially in HIV‑infected patients.
